summary: Defines a portion of the MIB for managing remote network monitoring devices, often called RMON. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1757.

eli5.summary: It is a checklist for little spy boxes that count and watch traffic on a network.

subtitle: Data definitions for managing remote network monitoring probes

tldr.problem: Network administrators needed a standard way to monitor remote network segments, but existing management protocols and MIBs did not provide the specialized data structures for monitoring probes.
tldr.mechanism: RMON MIB defines nine groups of data objects: Statistics, History, Alarm, Host, HostTopN, Matrix, Filter, Packet Capture, and Event. These groups provide a framework for monitoring devices to collect, store, and report network activity and errors.
tldr.outcome: The standard enabled the growth of dedicated network monitoring appliances that could operate independently and notify management stations of problems. RFC 1271 was later superseded by RFC 1757.

today: RFC 1271 was superseded by RFC 1757, which is the current RMON standard. RFC 1757 is widely implemented in network monitoring appliances and remains the foundation for remote network monitoring on IPv4 networks.

sections.title: Remote Network Monitoring Overview
sections.content:
A remote network monitoring device (often called a probe or RMON probe) is a stand-alone instrument placed on a network segment to observe and report on network activity. Unlike simple devices that only respond to management queries, remote monitoring probes can continuously collect statistics, detect problems, and notify a management station of anomalies even when the management station is not actively querying them.

This RFC defines the structure of the Remote Network Monitoring Management Information Base (RMON MIB), a set of data objects that a remote monitoring device must provide so that network management stations can retrieve its collected data via the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The RMON MIB is an extension to the existing network management framework defined in RFC 1213 (MIB-II).

Remote monitoring devices serve several key functions: offline operation (collecting data even when disconnected from the management station), preemptive monitoring (continuously running diagnostics and logging performance), problem detection and reporting (recognizing and notifying of error conditions), value-added data (preprocessing information to show, for example, which hosts generate the most traffic), and support for multiple management stations accessing the same probe.
sections.eli5: A probe is a little box on the network that watches everything and keeps notes. The RFC says what notes it must keep and how to ask for them.

sections.title: Nine Groups of Management Data
sections.content:
The RMON MIB organizes data into nine optional groups. Implementations can support any subset of these groups, but if a group is implemented, all objects within that group must be present.

The Statistics Group contains counters and statistics for each monitored network interface (currently Ethernet; future versions were planned to add Token Ring and FDDI). The History Group periodically collects snapshots of statistics and stores them for historical analysis and trend reporting.

The Alarm Group continuously monitors variables and compares them against configured thresholds. When a variable crosses a threshold, an event is triggered. A hysteresis mechanism prevents alarm storms by requiring the value to return within bounds before a new alarm can fire.

The Host Group discovers hosts on the network by observing the source and destination MAC addresses in network packets, then maintains statistics about the traffic and errors for each discovered host. The HostTopN Group builds reports ranking hosts by their traffic levels or error rates, allowing operators to quickly identify the busiest or most problematic stations.

The Matrix Group tracks statistics for conversations between pairs of hosts, recording bytes and packets sent between each pair in both directions. The Filter Group allows packets matching certain criteria to be selected for further processing or capture. The Packet Capture Group stores captured packets for detailed analysis by a management station.

The Event Group controls how alarms and other events are generated and logged, and determines which management stations should be notified and in what manner.
sections.eli5: The nine groups are like different kinds of reports: one counts packets, one remembers past activity, one watches for problems, one tracks hosts, one ranks them, one watches conversations, one filters packets, one saves them, and one says how to raise alarms.

sections.title: Control Tables and Data Tables
sections.content:
Each major functional group in RMON typically includes two types of tables: a control table and one or more data tables. The control table contains configuration parameters set by the management station to define what the probe should monitor or what actions it should take. Data tables contain the results—the counts, statistics, and captured data.

Control tables are read-write, allowing management stations to configure the probe's behavior. Data tables are typically read-only, since they contain results rather than configuration. To modify the parameters in a control entry, the management station invalidates the old entry (deleting it and any associated data), then creates a new control entry with the desired parameters. This approach cleanly separates configuration from results and prevents inconsistent states where the control parameters do not match the data being collected.

For example, the History Group has a historyControlTable (read-write) where operators specify which interface to monitor and how often to sample it, and etherHistoryTable (read-only) where the probe stores the collected samples.
sections.eli5: You fill in a form (control table) telling the probe what to watch, and then the probe puts its observations (data table) in a separate notebook.

sections.title: Sharing Probes Among Multiple Management Stations
sections.content:
Many organizations have multiple network management stations—for different departments, different functions (operations versus engineering), or for disaster recovery. When multiple management stations need to use the same remote monitoring probe, they must share finite resources: the probe's memory, processing power, and network bandwidth.

The RMON MIB includes mechanisms to manage this resource sharing. Each function initiated by a management station includes an owner label that identifies which management station owns that function. This allows a network operator to determine which station configured a particular alarm, history collection, or packet capture, and to contact them if resources need to be freed up.

The owner field also helps management stations recognize resources they configured in the past (useful after a crash and restart) and allows operators to clean up abandoned resources if a management station crashes without properly releasing them.

Different management stations can work concurrently on the same probe using different groups or different instances of the same group without interfering with each other, as long as the probe has sufficient resources.
sections.eli5: If several managers use the same spy camera, they mark which alarms they set up so they can find them again later.

sections.title: Using the RMON MIB
sections.content:
The RMON MIB is defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI) and Abstract Syntax Notation (ASN.1), the same formal language used for all SNMP MIBs. Each object has a name (object identifier), a data type (syntax), and semantics defining its meaning and use.

The document specifies two new textual conventions for RMON: OwnerString (to identify the owner of a function) and EntryStatus (to control the lifecycle of table entries and trigger actions).

Implementations must also support the system and interfaces groups from MIB-II and may be required to support additional groups depending on the probe's capabilities. The RFC is structured with each group defined as a base unit of conformance—if a probe claims to implement a group, it must implement every object in that group.
sections.eli5: The RFC uses a formal language to precisely describe each piece of data the probe collects, like a blueprint for the information.
